danish.title: Fjortende bog (1812) — Kapitel 14
paragraphs: »À vos places!« * lød pludselig en stemme.
* »På plads!«

En behagelig følelse af spænding og forventning om noget glædeligt og højtideligt bredte sig blandt eskortesoldaterne og fangerne. Fra alle sider lød kommandoråb, og fra venstre kom velklædte kavalerisoldater på gode heste, der passerede fangerne i trav. Alles ansigtsudtryk viste den anspændthed, folk føler, når myndighederne nærmer sig. Fangerne trængtes sammen og blev skubbet væk fra vejen. Eskorten stillede op.

»Kejseren! Kejseren! Marskalken! Hertugen!« Og næppe var det elegante kavaleri redet forbi, før en vogn trukket af seks grå heste raslede forbi. Pierre fik et glimt af en mand i en trekantet hat med et roligt udtryk i sit smukke, fyldige, hvide ansigt. Det var en af marskalkerne. Hans blik faldt på Pierres store og iøjnefaldende skikkelse, og i det udtryk, hvormed han rynkede panden og kiggede væk, syntes Pierre at spore medfølelse og et ønske om at skjule den medfølelse.

Generalen med ansvaret for forsyningerne galopperede efter vognen med et rødt og skræmt ansigt, mens han piskede sin magre hest. Flere officerer dannede en gruppe, og nogle soldater stimlede sammen om dem. Deres ansigter så alle ophidsede og bekymrede ud.
»Hvad sagde han? Hvad sagde han?« hørte Pierre dem spørge.

Mens marskalken passerede forbi, var fangerne trængt sammen i en klynge, og Pierre så Karatajev, som han endnu ikke havde set den morgen. Han sad i sin korte frakke, lænende sig op ad et birketræ. Hans ansigt bar, foruden det udtryk af glad bevægelse, det havde haft i går, da han fortalte historien om den købmand, der led uskyldigt, nu et præg af stille højtidelighed.

Karatajev så på Pierre med sine venlige, runde øjne, nu fyldte med tårer, og ville tydeligvis gerne, at Pierre skulle komme nærmere, så han kunne sige ham noget. Men Pierre var ikke sikker nok på sig selv. Han lod, som om han ikke havde bemærket det blik, og gik hurtigt videre.

Da fangerne igen satte sig i bevægelse, kiggede Pierre sig om. Karatajev sad stadig ved vejkanten under birketræet, og to franskmænd talte hen over hans hoved. Pierre kiggede sig ikke mere om, men gik haltende op ad bakken.

Bagfra, dér hvor Karatajev havde siddet, lød et skud. Pierre hørte det tydeligt, men i det øjeblik huskede han, at han endnu ikke var færdig med at regne ud, hvor mange dagsmarcher der stadig var til Smolensk — en beregning han var begyndt på, inden marskalken passerede. Og han begyndte igen at tælle. To franske soldater løb forbi Pierre, den ene med et sænket og rygende gevær. De så begge blege ud, og i udtrykket på deres ansigter — den ene kastede et sky blik på Pierre — var der noget, der mindede om det, han havde set i den unge soldats ansigt ved henrettelsen. Pierre kiggede på soldaten og mindedes, at manden to dage forinden havde brændt sin skjorte, mens han tørrede den ved ilden, og hvordan de havde grinet af ham.
Bagfra, dér hvor Karatajev havde siddet, begyndte hunden at tude. »Sikke et dumt dyr! Hvorfor tuder den?« tænkte Pierre.

Hans kammerater, de tilfangetagne soldater der gik ved hans side, undgik at kigge tilbage mod det sted, hvor skuddet var faldet og hunden tudede, ligesom Pierre, men der lå et fast udtryk i alles ansigter.

english.title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 14
paragraphs: "To your places!" a voice suddenly cried.
"To your places!"

A pleasant feeling of excitement and an expectation of something important and grand arose among both the convoy soldiers and the prisoners. From all sides came shouts of command, and from the left came smartly dressed cavalrymen on good horses, passing the prisoners at a trot. Every face showed the tension people feel at the approach of someone in authority. The prisoners crowded together and were pushed off the road. The convoy formed up.

"The Emperor! The Emperor! The Marshal! The Duke!" And hardly had the sleek cavalry passed before a carriage drawn by six gray horses rattled by. Pierre caught a glimpse of a man in a three-cornered hat with a calm expression on his handsome, plump, white face. It was one of the marshals. His eye fell on Pierre's large and striking figure, and in the expression with which he frowned and looked away, Pierre thought he detected sympathy and a desire to hide it.

The general in charge of the stores galloped after the carriage, red-faced and frightened, whipping up his thin horse. Several officers formed a group and some soldiers crowded around them. Their faces all looked excited and worried.
"What did he say? What did he say?" Pierre heard them asking.

While the marshal was passing, the prisoners had huddled together in a crowd, and Pierre saw Karataev, whom he hadn't yet seen that morning. He sat in his short overcoat, leaning against a birch tree. On his face, besides the look of joyful emotion it had worn the night before while he told the story of the merchant who suffered innocently, there was now an expression of quiet solemnity.

Karataev looked at Pierre with his kind, round eyes, now filled with tears, clearly wanting him to come closer so he could say something. But Pierre wasn't sure enough of himself. He acted as if he hadn't noticed that look and moved quickly away.

When the prisoners started walking again, Pierre looked back. Karataev was still sitting at the side of the road under the birch tree, and two Frenchmen were talking over his head. Pierre didn't look back again, but went limping up the hill.

From behind, where Karataev had been sitting, came the sound of a shot. Pierre heard it clearly, but at that moment he remembered he hadn't yet finished calculating how many stages remained to Smolensk—a calculation he had begun before the marshal went by. And he started counting again. Two French soldiers ran past Pierre, one of them carrying a lowered and still-smoking gun. They both looked pale, and in the expression on their faces—one of them glanced nervously at Pierre—there was something resembling what he had seen on the face of the young soldier at the execution. Pierre looked at the soldier and remembered that two days earlier, that man had burned his shirt while drying it at the fire and everyone had laughed at him.
Behind him, where Karataev had been sitting, the dog began to howl. "What a stupid animal! Why is it howling?" thought Pierre.

His comrades, the prisoner soldiers walking beside him, avoided looking back at the place where the shot had been fired and the dog was howling, just as Pierre did. But there was a fixed look on all their faces.
